q: Dioxygen can be prepared by thermal decomposition of
question: Dioxygen can be prepared by thermal decomposition of
solution:
1. Barium peroxide ($\text{BaO}_2$):

When barium peroxide is heated strongly, it loses oxygen and forms barium oxide:

$$2\text{BaO}_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{BaO} + \text{O}_2$$

This reaction releases dioxygen gas.

  1. Potassium nitrate ($\text{KNO}_3$):

Alkali metal nitrates (like $\text{NaNO}_3$ and $\text{KNO}_3$) decompose on heating to form the corresponding metal nitrite and liberate oxygen gas:

$$2\text{KNO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{KNO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$

Dioxygen is evolved in this reaction as well.

  1. Lithium nitrate ($\text{LiNO}_3$):

Because of its small size and high polarizing power, the lithium ion shows anomalous behavior compared to other alkali metals. On heating, lithium nitrate decomposes to form lithium oxide, nitrogen dioxide, and oxygen gas:

$$4\text{LiNO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{Li}_2\text{O} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$

Dioxygen gas is produced here too.

Since all three compounds release dioxygen upon thermal decomposition, the correct choice is Option D (all of these).

question: Ozone is
options: identified by its characteristic rotten egg smell.
used to identify the structures of unsaturated compounds.
not used for disinfecting or sterilizing water.
solution:
• Option A: Ozone has a characteristic pungent odor, whereas a "rotten egg smell" is the classic identifying characteristic of hydrogen sulfide ($H_2S$).

  • Option B: Ozone is quantitatively estimated and typically identified using an aqueous solution of potassium iodide (KI), which it oxidizes to liberate iodine ($I_2$), rather than being identified by $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{SO}_3$.

  • Option C: Ozone readily reacts with unsaturated compounds (alkenes and alkynes) to form ozonides. Through a process called ozonolysis, these ozonides are cleaved to form carbonyl compounds. Identifying these resulting fragments allows chemists to determine the exact position of the double or triple bonds in the original molecule.

  • Option D: Because ozone is a powerful oxidizing agent that leaves no chemical residue, it is widely used as a germicide and disinfectant for sterilizing drinking water.

The correct statement is Option C.

q:
The correct order of S—S bond length in following oxyanions is :

(I) $\mathrm{S_2O_4^{2-}}$ (II) $\mathrm{S_2O_5^{2-}}$ (III) $\mathrm{S_2O_6^{2-}}$
question:
The correct order of S—S bond length in following oxyanions is :

(I) $\mathrm{S_2O_4^{2-}}$ (II) $\mathrm{S_2O_5^{2-}}$ (III) $\mathrm{S_2O_6^{2-}}$
solution:
To compare the $\mathrm{S-S}$ bond lengths, let us look at the structures and the environment around the sulfur atoms in each oxyanion:

1. Dithionite ion $(\mathrm{S_2O_4^{2-}})$:

Each sulfur atom has a lone pair of electrons. The repulsion between these two lone pairs significantly weakens and lengthens the $\mathrm{S-S}$ bond ($X_1 \approx 239\text{ pm}$).

2. Disulfite ion $(\mathrm{S_2O_5^{2-}})$:

Only one sulfur atom has a lone pair, reducing the lone pair repulsion compared to $\mathrm{S_2O_4^{2-}}$. As a result, the $\mathrm{S-S}$ bond is shorter ($X_2 \approx 222\text{ pm}$).

3. Dithionate ion $(\mathrm{S_2O_6^{2-}})$:

Neither sulfur atom has a lone pair. According to Bent's rule, the electronegative oxygen atoms draw more p-character into the $\mathrm{S-O}$ bonds, leaving higher s-character in the central $\mathrm{S-S}$ bond. Higher s-character makes this bond the shortest and strongest ($X_3 \approx 215\text{ pm}$).

Comparing the lengths gives the order:

$$X_1 > X_2 > X_3$$

Thus, the correct order of $\mathrm{S-S}$ bond length is:

$$\mathrm{S_2O_4^{2-}} > \mathrm{S_2O_5^{2-}} > \mathrm{S_2O_6^{2-}} \quad \text{i.e.,} \quad \text{(I)} > \text{(II)} > \text{(III)}$$

q:
Arrange the following species according to their bond angle order:

(I) O3 (II) NO2− (III) FNO
question:
Arrange the following species according to their bond angle order:

(I) O3 (II) NO2− (III) FNO
solution:
1. Ozone ($\text{O}_3$)

The central oxygen atom forms one double bond and one single (coordinate) bond with the surrounding oxygen atoms, and it retains one lone pair:

$$\text{O}=\overset{+}{\text{O}}-\text{O}^-$$

  • The steric number of the central atom is $2\ (\sigma\text{ bonds}) + 1\ (\text{lone pair}) = 3$, giving $sp^2$ hybridisation with a bent shape.

  • The ideal angle for $sp^2$ hybridisation is $120^\circ$.

  • The central oxygen carries a formal positive charge, which pulls the lone pair closer to its nucleus. This reduces the repulsion between the lone pair and the bond pairs.

  • As a result, the bond angle is only slightly reduced from $120^\circ$ to approximately $116.8^\circ$.

2. Nitrite ion ($\text{NO}_2^-$)

The central nitrogen atom has 5 valence electrons, and the negative charge adds one more electron, making a total of 6 valence electrons:

  • Nitrogen forms two $\sigma$ bonds with the oxygen atoms and has one lone pair.

  • The steric number is $2 + 1 = 3$, which corresponds to $sp^2$ hybridisation and a bent shape.

  • Due to the net negative charge on the ion, the electron density on the lone pair is higher compared to that in ozone, causing greater lone pair–bond pair repulsion.

  • This pushes the bonds closer together, making the bond angle approximately $115.4^\circ$.

3. Nitrosyl fluoride ($\text{FNO}$)

The central atom is nitrogen:

  • Nitrogen forms a single bond with fluorine ($\text{F}$), a double bond with oxygen ($\text{O}$), and possesses one lone pair.

  • The steric number is $2 + 1 = 3$, so it is also $sp^2$ hybridised with a bent shape.

  • Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so it strongly pulls the bonding electron pair of the $\text{N}-\text{F}$ bond away from the central nitrogen atom.

  • This significantly reduces the repulsion between the bonding electron pairs, allowing the lone pair to push the bonds much closer together.

  • Consequently, the $\text{F}-\text{N}=\text{O}$ bond angle decreases sharply to about $110^\circ$.

Comparing the bond angles:

$$\text{O}_3\ (116.8^\circ) > \text{NO}_2^-\ (115.4^\circ) > \text{FNO}\ (110^\circ)$$

This gives the order:

$$\text{I} > \text{II} > \text{III}$$

Therefore, the correct option is Option A.

q:
Which of the following halides cannot be hydrolysed at room temperature?

(I) TeF6 (II) SF6 (III) NCl3 (IV) NF3

Choose the correct code:
question:
Which of the following halides cannot be hydrolysed at room temperature?

(I) TeF6 (II) SF6 (III) NCl3 (IV) NF3

Choose the correct code:
solution:
1. $\text{TeF}_6$

Tellurium has a relatively large size and vacant d-orbitals. Because of the large size of the central tellurium atom, steric hindrance is low, and water molecules can easily attack it. Thus, $\text{TeF}_6$ gets hydrolysed at room temperature to give telluric acid:

$$\text{TeF}_6 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_6\text{TeO}_6 + 6\text{HF}$$

2. $\text{SF}_6$

In $\text{SF}_6$, the sulfur atom is small and completely shielded by six highly electronegative fluorine atoms. This creates strong steric crowding, which prevents water molecules from attacking the central sulfur atom. In addition, the $\text{S}-\text{F}$ bond is extremely strong. Therefore, $\text{SF}_6$ is chemically inert and cannot be hydrolysed at room temperature.

3. $\text{NCl}_3$

Although the central nitrogen atom has no vacant d-orbitals, the chlorine atoms have vacant d-orbitals. A water molecule can donate its lone pair to a chlorine atom, leading to hydrolysis at room temperature:

$$\text{NCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + 3\text{HOCl}$$

4. $\text{NF}_3$

In $\text{NF}_3$, neither nitrogen nor fluorine has vacant d-orbitals in their valence shells to accept the lone pair of electrons from water. Furthermore, the $\text{N}-\text{F}$ bond is very strong and stable. Because there is no pathway for attack, $\text{NF}_3$ does not undergo hydrolysis.

Therefore, the halides that cannot be hydrolysed at room temperature are $\text{SF}_6$ (II)$ and \text{NF}_3$ (IV).

Correct Option: Option D

q: Which of the following forms of SO3 exists as a cyclic trimer(s)?
question: Which of the following forms of SO3 exists as a cyclic trimer(s)?
solution:
Solid sulfur trioxide ($\text{SO}_3$) exists in three main crystalline forms: $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$.

  • $\gamma\text{-SO}_3$ is an ice-like solid. It is made of discrete cyclic trimers, $(\text{SO}_3)_3$, having the molecular formula $\text{S}_3\text{O}_9$. In this structure, sulfur and oxygen atoms alternate to form a puckered six-membered ring.

  • $\beta\text{-SO}_3$ is an asbestos-like, fibrous solid consisting of infinite helical polymeric chains.

  • $\alpha\text{-SO}_3$ has the most complex, cross-linked sheet-like polymeric network and is the most stable form.

Because the cyclic trimer structure belongs to the $\gamma$-form, the correct choice is:

Option C: $\gamma\text{-SO}_3$

q: Which of the following chemical reactions depicts the oxidising behaviour of $H_2SO_4$?
question: Which of the following chemical reactions depicts the oxidising behaviour of $H_2SO_4$?
solution:
The reaction that shows the oxidising behaviour of $H_2SO_4$ is:

$$ 2HI + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow I_2 + SO_2 + 2H_2O $$

So, the correct option is Option A.

Here, concentrated $H_2SO_4$ acts as an oxidising agent.

In $HI$, iodine is present as iodide ion, $I^-$, with oxidation state $-1$.

In $I_2$, iodine has oxidation state $0$.

So iodine is oxidised:

$$ I^- \rightarrow I_2 $$

At the same time, sulphur in $H_2SO_4$ has oxidation state $+6$.

In $SO_2$, sulphur has oxidation state $+4$.

So sulphur is reduced:

$$ H_2SO_4 \rightarrow SO_2 $$

Since $H_2SO_4$ gets reduced and oxidises $HI$ to $I_2$, it is showing oxidising behaviour.

Hence, the answer is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option A}} $$

q: Gas that can not be collected over water is :
question: Gas that can not be collected over water is :
solution:
To collect a gas over water by the downward displacement of water, the gas must satisfy two basic conditions:

  1. It should not be highly soluble in water.

  2. It should not react chemically with water.

Let us look at the given gases:

Nitrogen ($\text{N}_2$) and oxygen ($\text{O}_2$) are non-polar molecules and are only very sparingly soluble in water. They do not react with water at room temperature, so both can be collected over water.

Phosphine ($\text{PH}_3$) is also sparingly soluble in water and does not react with it under normal conditions, so it can be collected over water as well.

Sulphur dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$) is extremely soluble in water. When it comes into contact with water, it readily dissolves and reacts chemically to form sulphurous acid:

$$\text{SO}_2\text{ (g)} + \text{H}_2\text{O (l)} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{SO}_3\text{ (aq)}$$

Because $\text{SO}_2$ dissolves and reacts so quickly, it cannot be collected over water. Instead, it is usually collected by the upward displacement of air or over mercury.

The correct option is Option C ($\text{SO}_2$).

q: In which of the following reaction product does not contain 'Peroxy' linkage?
question: In which of the following reaction product does not contain 'Peroxy' linkage?
solution:
In Option A, the dimerisation of $\text{OF}$ radicals takes place:

$$2\text{OF} \longrightarrow \text{O}_2\text{F}_2$$

The structure of dioxygen difluoride is $\text{F}-\text{O}-\text{O}-\text{F}$.

A true peroxy linkage $(-\text{O}-\text{O}-)$ requires the oxygen atoms to have an oxidation state of $-1$, which occurs when oxygen is bonded to elements that are less electronegative than itself. In $\text{O}_2\text{F}_2$, fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen. As a result, fluorine has an oxidation state of $-1$ and each oxygen atom has an oxidation state of $+1$. Because oxygen is in a positive oxidation state, $\text{O}_2\text{F}_2$ is classified as an oxygen fluoride and does not contain a peroxy linkage.

In Option B, peroxodiphosphoric acid undergoes hydrolysis:

$$\text{H}_4\text{P}_2\text{O}_8 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_5 + \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$

On further hydrolysis:

$$\text{H}_3\text{PO}_5 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2$$

Both peroxomonophosphoric acid ($\text{H}_3\text{PO}_5$) and hydrogen peroxide ($\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$) contain the peroxy linkage $(-\text{O}-\text{O}-)$ where oxygen has an oxidation state of $-1$.

In Option C, sodium reacts with excess oxygen on heating to form sodium peroxide:

$$2\text{Na} + \text{O}_2(\text{excess}) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$$

Sodium peroxide consists of $\text{Na}^+$ ions and the peroxide ion, $[\text{O}-\text{O}]^{2-}$, where the oxygen atoms have an oxidation state of $-1$. Thus, it contains a peroxy linkage.

Therefore, the product in Option A does not contain a peroxy linkage.

q:
How many of the following properties increase regularly from $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ to $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Te}$ ?

(i) Acidic strength

(ii) Bond angle

(iii) Boiling point

(iv) Bond length ( $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{E}$ )
question:
How many of the following properties increase regularly from $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ to $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Te}$ ?

(i) Acidic strength

(ii) Bond angle

(iii) Boiling point

(iv) Bond length ( $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{E}$ )
solution:
• (i) Acidic strength: As you move down the group from oxygen to tellurium, the atomic size of the central atom (E) increases. This causes the $H-E$ bond to become longer and weaker, meaning the bond dissociation enthalpy decreases. Consequently, it becomes easier to release an $H^+$ ion. Therefore, acidic strength increases regularly down the group ($H_2O < H_2S < H_2Se < H_2Te$).

  • (ii) Bond angle: As you move down the group, the electronegativity of the central atom decreases. This causes the shared electron pairs in the $H-E$ bonds to lie further away from the central atom, which reduces the bond pair-bond pair repulsion. Therefore, the bond angle decreases down the group ($H_2O \approx 104.5^\circ$, $H_2S \approx 92^\circ$, $H_2Se \approx 91^\circ$, $H_2Te \approx 90^\circ$).

  • (iii) Boiling point: Due to its small size and high electronegativity, oxygen forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds in water ($H_2O$), giving it an exceptionally high boiling point. For the subsequent hydrides, boiling point increases with molecular mass due to increasing van der Waals forces ($H_2S < H_2Se < H_2Te < H_2O$). Therefore, the boiling point does not increase regularly.

  • (iv) Bond length ($H-E$): As the principal quantum number increases down the group, the atomic radius of the central atom increases significantly. This directly results in the $H-E$ bond length increasing regularly from $H_2O$ to $H_2Te$.

There are exactly 2 properties (acidic strength and bond length) that increase regularly from $H_2O$ to $H_2Te$.

The correct integer answer is 2.

• (i) Acidic strength: As you move down the group from oxygen to tellurium, the atomic size of the central atom (E) increases. This causes the $H-E$ bond to become longer and weaker, meaning the bond dissociation enthalpy decreases. Consequently, it becomes easier to release an $H^+$ ion. Therefore, acidic strength increases regularly down the group ($H_2O < H_2S < H_2Se < H_2Te$).

  • (ii) Bond angle: As you move down the group, the electronegativity of the central atom decreases. This causes the shared electron pairs in the $H-E$ bonds to lie further away from the central atom, which reduces the bond pair-bond pair repulsion. Therefore, the bond angle decreases down the group ($H_2O \approx 104.5^\circ$, $H_2S \approx 92^\circ$, $H_2Se \approx 91^\circ$, $H_2Te \approx 90^\circ$).

  • (iii) Boiling point: Due to its small size and high electronegativity, oxygen forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds in water ($H_2O$), giving it an exceptionally high boiling point. For the subsequent hydrides, boiling point increases with molecular mass due to increasing van der Waals forces ($H_2S < H_2Se < H_2Te < H_2O$). Therefore, the boiling point does not increase regularly.

  • (iv) Bond length ($H-E$): As the principal quantum number increases down the group, the atomic radius of the central atom increases significantly. This directly results in the $H-E$ bond length increasing regularly from $H_2O$ to $H_2Te$.

There are exactly 2 properties (acidic strength and bond length) that increase regularly from $H_2O$ to $H_2Te$.

The correct integer answer is 2.

q: The atomic number of group-16 element, which show only +2 and +4 oxidation state is ……
question: The atomic number of group-16 element, which show only +2 and +4 oxidation state is ……
solution:
• Group 16 Elements: The elements in this group are Oxygen (O), Sulphur (S), Selenium (Se), Tellurium (Te), and Polonium (Po).

  • General Oxidation States: The common oxidation states for Group 16 elements are -2, +2, +4, and +6.

  • Trends down the Group:

  • The stability of the -2 oxidation state decreases down the group due to a decrease in electronegativity and an increase in metallic character. Polonium, being a metal, hardly shows a -2 oxidation state.

  • The stability of the +6 oxidation state decreases and the stability of the +4 oxidation state increases down the group. This is due to the inert pair effect, where the outermost s-electrons become more reluctant to participate in bonding.

  • Identifying the Element: In Polonium (Po), the inert pair effect is the strongest. As a result, it does not exhibit the +6 oxidation state. Combined with its inability to show the -2 state, Polonium primarily exhibits only the +2 and +4 oxidation states.

  • Atomic Number: The element is Polonium (Po), which has an atomic number of 84.

The atomic number of the group-16 element is 84.

q: How many $\pi$-bonds are present in Marshall's acid?
question: How many $\pi$-bonds are present in Marshall's acid?
solution:
• Chemical Identity: Marshall's acid is the common name for peroxydisulphuric acid, which has the chemical formula $H_2S_2O_8$.

  • Structural Arrangement: The molecule features two central sulphur atoms connected by a peroxy linkage ($-O-O-$).

  • Bonding: Each sulphur atom is tetrahedrally surrounded and bonded to:

  • One peroxy oxygen (single bond)

  • One hydroxyl ($-OH$) group (single bond)

  • Two oxygen atoms via double bonds ($S=O$)

  • Counting $\pi$-bonds: A double bond consists of one $\sigma$-bond and one $\pi$-bond.

  • Each sulphur atom forms two $S=O$ double bonds, contributing 2 $\pi$-bonds.

  • Because there are two sulphur atoms in the molecule, there are a total of $2 \times 2 = 4$ double bonds.

Therefore, the total number of $\pi$-bonds present in Marshall's acid is 4.

The correct integer answer is 4.

$\begin{aligned} \text { How many statements about } \mathrm{O}}_{3} \text { are correct? }\\ \text { (i) } \mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O} \text { bond lengths are equal. }\\ \text { (ii) Thermal decomposition of } \mathrm{O}}_{3} \text { is endothermic. }\\ \text { (iii) } \mathrm{O}}_{3} \text { is diamagnetic in nature. }\\ \text { (iv) } \mathrm{O}}_{3} \text { has a bent structure. }
\end{aligned}$
question:
$\begin{aligned} \text { How many statements about } \mathrm{O}}_{3} \text { are correct? }\\ \text { (i) } \mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O} \text { bond lengths are equal. }\\ \text { (ii) Thermal decomposition of } \mathrm{O}}_{3} \text { is endothermic. }\\ \text { (iii) } \mathrm{O}}_{3} \text { is diamagnetic in nature. }\\ \text { (iv) } \mathrm{O}}_{3} \text { has a bent structure. }
\end{aligned}$
solution:
Statement (i): $\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O}$ bond lengths are equal.
Due to resonance, the two $\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O}$ bonds are identical, with an intermediate bond length of about $128\text{ pm}$. So, this statement is correct.

Statement (ii): Thermal decomposition of $\mathrm{O}_3$ is endothermic.
The decomposition of ozone into oxygen: $$2\mathrm{O}_3(\text{g}) \rightarrow 3\mathrm{O}_2(\text{g})$$ releases heat ($\Delta H < 0$), which means it is an exothermic reaction, not endothermic. So, this statement is incorrect.

Statement (iii): $\mathrm{O}_3$ is diamagnetic in nature.
All the electrons in the ozone molecule are paired, so it has no unpaired electrons and is diamagnetic. So, this statement is correct.

Statement (iv): $\mathrm{O}_3$ has a bent structure.
The central oxygen atom undergoes $sp^2$ hybridisation and has one lone pair, giving the molecule an angular or bent shape with a bond angle of about $117^\circ$. So, this statement is correct.

Therefore, 3 statements (i, iii, and iv) are correct.
